title: The NEET Leak Network: From a Pune Professor’s Living Room to a Sikar WhatsApp Group, the CBI Maps India’s Biggest Exam Scandal
excerpt: The cancellation of NEET-UG 2026 on May 3 sent 22.79 lakh students into freefall. Two weeks later, the CBI has arrested seven people, traced the leak to a biology lecturer on NTA’s own paper-setting committee, and uncovered a multi-state pipeline that sold exam papers for ₹2–60 lakh a copy.
body:
On the evening of May 3, the National Testing Agency did something it has never done before: it cancelled NEET-UG, India’s single gateway to medical college, after concluding that the exam’s integrity had been fatally compromised. Two weeks and seven arrests later, the Central Bureau of Investigation has pieced together a leak network that stretches from a Pune professor’s coaching sessions to a Rajasthani town’s WhatsApp groups — and the trail is still growing.

## The Kingpin in the Classroom

At the centre of the CBI’s case is Prahalad Vishnu Kulkarni, a chemistry professor based in Pune whom investigators have described as the operation’s kingpin. Kulkarni allegedly obtained a hard copy of the biology paper — the section carrying the most marks — and organised pre-exam coaching sessions where students were walked through the actual questions. Manisha Mandhare, a biology lecturer who served on NTA’s own paper-setting expert committee, was arrested for allegedly leaking the botany and zoology sections she had helped create.

The CBI has now placed both in ten-day judicial custody. A Delhi court noted “ongoing investigations into a larger conspiracy involving multiple suspects,” suggesting that the probe is far from over.

## The Distribution Chain

What makes this scandal different from India’s long history of exam leaks is the sophistication of the distribution pipeline. According to CBI filings, the leaked paper moved through at least four stages: a hard copy originating in Pune was scanned and converted to handwritten notes, then distributed via WhatsApp and Telegram groups to middlemen in Rajasthan and Maharashtra, who in turn sold access to students — or, more accurately, to their parents — for sums ranging from ₹2 lakh to ₹60 lakh.

Sikar, a dusty district in northern Rajasthan that has become India’s unofficial coaching capital, sits at the hub of the network. CBI teams have raided 14 locations across the country, visited the Jaipur home of accused middlemen Mangilal and Dinesh Biwal, and are analysing seized phones and laptops for forensic evidence. One detail, darkly comic, has caught public attention: a Sikar man allegedly paid ₹10 lakh for his son to receive the leaked paper. The son scored 107 out of 720.

## 22.79 Lakh in Limbo

The human cost is staggering. NEET-UG 2026 was sat by 22.79 lakh students — nearly 2.3 million young people, most of them 17 or 18 years old, who had spent one to three years in gruelling preparation. NTA has confirmed a re-examination will be held, with no fresh registration required and fees refunded, but a new date has not been set. The agency has also signalled a future shift to Computer-Based Testing, an acknowledgment that the pen-and-paper format is now considered too vulnerable to breach.

For students, the psychological toll is incalculable. Online forums and coaching-centre WhatsApp groups are flooded with anxiety, anger, and conspiracy theories. Parents — many of whom took loans to fund NEET coaching — are demanding accountability not just from the accused but from NTA itself, whose vetting of its own expert committee members is now under the harshest scrutiny in the agency’s history.

## The NRI Dimension

In Indian-American households from New Jersey to the Bay Area, the NEET scandal has reopened a wound that never fully healed. Many first-generation NRIs left India in part because they saw competitive exams — and the corruption surrounding them — as a rigged game. Now, with children who hold OCI cards and are eligible to sit Indian medical entrance exams, the system’s fragility is personal again.

Diaspora medical associations have called for an independent audit of NTA’s security protocols. Some have gone further, arguing that India’s centralised testing model — one exam, one day, one shot for millions — is structurally incapable of preventing leaks at scale. The comparison to the SAT and MCAT, which are administered in smaller, more frequent cohorts with adaptive testing, has resurfaced with renewed force.

## What Comes Next

The CBI’s investigation is expanding. Investigators are probing potential links between the leak network and NTA officials beyond Mandhare, and forensic analysis of seized devices is ongoing. The re-exam, whenever it is scheduled, will face unprecedented logistical and security demands. And in Sikar’s cramped coaching hostels, 17-year-olds who already sat the exam once are picking up their textbooks again, bracing for round two — this time with the knowledge that the system they trusted was never quite as secure as they were told.
